scope: Missing labor prisoners identified during CIO and related WPA custody review; existing profiles preserved.

maine_court.label: Maine Reports 135, Charles Cushman Co. v. Mackesy, pp.490-500 (PDF pp.502-512), June 30, 1938; contempt sentence and dismissal for unverified petitions. Relevant custody/charge page491 visually reviewed.

call_june.label: Socialist Call, June 26, 1937, p.12, Norman Thomas, The Shoe Workers Strike in Maine. Contemporary visit account, including Ernest Henry kept three weeks; visually reviewed.

call_july.label: Socialist Call, July 31, 1937, p.2, Strike for Closed Shop Illegal in N.J. Reports Maine organizers and attorney Sidney Grant released on bail after about two months; visually reviewed.

oneil_ap.label: Medford Mail Tribune, April 30, 1941, p.12, AP report of James D. O'Neil contempt sentence and continued custody; university archive full text. His illness explanation and the judge's contrary conclusion are kept distinct.

oneil_union.label: Voice of the Federation, May 3, 1941, p.8, Jailed For Attacking Frame-up. Actual continuing jail custody; visually reviewed. Union allegations of a frame-up are not adopted as independent findings.

nw_feb8.label: Northwest Organizer, February 8, 1940, p.1. Named sentences and report that sentenced WPA defendants were back in county jail receiving milk; visually reviewed.

nw_feb15.label: Northwest Organizer, February 15, 1940, pp.1,3. Minnie Kohn workhouse entry, male prisoner transfer, and explicit February 3 start of terms; visually reviewed. Page3 differs from headline on collective count; no unnamed person is inferred.

dobbs_1975.label: Farrell Dobbs, Teamster history excerpt, The Militant, May 9, 1975, pp.14-15. Max Geldman recollection explicitly confirms Minnie Kohn served her time. Sentence discrepancies held in audit; page15 visually reviewed.

prisoner.name: William J. Mackesy
prisoner.description: William J. Mackesy was a shoe-worker strike organizer jailed during the 1937 Lewiston-Auburn shoe strike for violating an injunction against support for the strike.

cases.charges: Contempt of court — support for the 1937 shoe strike in violation of an injunction
cases.sentence: Six months in jail. Contemporary reporting confirms actual custody and later release on bail after about two months. The contempt proceedings were dismissed June 30, 1938 for lack of verified petitions. Exact custody endpoints remain unresolved.

prisoner.aka: William Mackesy; William J. Macksey; William Macksey

entries.custody_evidence: The court identifies the contempt defendants. The July 31 newspaper confirms the organizers and their attorney served about two months before bail.

case_research.custody_evidence: The court identifies the contempt defendants. The July 31 newspaper confirms the organizers and their attorney served about two months before bail.

entries.status_research: Do not equate the separate riot/conspiracy prosecution with the contempt proceeding or treat the 1938 disposition as the jail release date. About two months is approximate, not an exact counter value.

prisoner.name: James D. O'Neil
prisoner.description: James D. O'Neil was a former West Coast CIO publicity director jailed for contempt during the 1941 Harry Bridges deportation hearing after failing to appear when summoned. O'Neil said he had been ill; the court rejected that explanation.

cases.charges: Contempt of court — failure to appear as a summoned witness in the Harry Bridges deportation hearing
cases.sentence: Sixty-day county-jail sentence imposed April 30, 1941. Continued custody was ordered despite a stay of execution; the May 3 union newspaper confirms he was serving the term. Actual release and full duration remain unverified.

entries.custody_evidence: The April 30 AP report says he would remain in custody; the May 3 union newspaper confirms ongoing service, establishing multiple days.

case_research.custody_evidence: The April 30 AP report says he would remain in custody; the May 3 union newspaper confirms ongoing service, establishing multiple days.

prisoner.name: Leslie Wachter
prisoner.description: Leslie Wachter was a Minneapolis WPA striker imprisoned following the 1939 strike against changes to federal work-relief conditions.

cases.charges: Federal prosecution arising from the 1939 WPA strike; individual count details unresolved
cases.sentence: Eight months plus eighteen months probation. The February 1940 union reports confirm actual custody beginning February 3. Exact release and completed duration remain unverified.

entries.custody_evidence: The February 8 named roster and milk-delivery report confirm county-jail custody after sentencing. February 15 page3 explicitly dates the start of terms to February 3 and reports continuing confinement or transfer.

case_research.custody_evidence: The February 8 named roster and milk-delivery report confirm county-jail custody after sentencing. February 15 page3 explicitly dates the start of terms to February 3 and reports continuing confinement or transfer.

entries.status_research: The contemporary February 8 paper says eight months; the 1975 Dobbs account says one year and one day. Keep the contemporary figure attributed; no actual eight-month total or inferred release. Group transfer to Sandstone reported February 15; collective counts conflict. No individual institution ID or transfer date inferred.

prisoner.name: Minnie Kohn
prisoner.description: Minnie Kohn was a Minneapolis WPA sewing-project striker jailed after the 1939 strike. She was the only woman among the fourteen sentenced in February 1940 to receive an unsuspended jail term.

cases.charges: Conspiracy arising from the 1939 WPA strike
cases.sentence: Forty-five days in the city workhouse. Contemporary reporting places sentencing and workhouse entry on February 10, 1940; participant Max Geldman later confirmed she served her time. Exact release date remains unresolved.

entries.custody_evidence: February 15 page3 reports Kohn was taken to the workhouse after Saturday sentencing. The 1975 participant recollection explicitly states she served her time and came out; the other thirteen women received probation.

case_research.custody_evidence: February 15 page3 reports Kohn was taken to the workhouse after Saturday sentencing. The 1975 participant recollection explicitly states she served her time and came out; the other thirteen women received probation.

research_notes: No inferred vital dates, release endpoints, photos or individual institution links. Later recollection used for actual Kohn service; sentence conflicts documented.
